segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you yourselves know, brothers and sisters, that our visit to you has not proved empty,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated in Philippi, as you know, we found boldness in our God to speak to you the good news of God amid a great struggle.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For our appeal does not come from error or from impurity, nor is it made with deceit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but just as we have been tested and found fit by God to be entrusted with the good news, so we speak, not to please people but to please God, who tests our hearts.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we never came with flattering speech, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: though as apostles of Christ we could have made our weight felt. But we were gentle among you, like a nurse cherishing her own children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Longing for you so, we were glad to share with you not only the good news of God but our own lives as well, because you had become dear to us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you remember, brothers and sisters, our labor and toil: working night and day so as not to weigh on any of you, we proclaimed to you the good news of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You are witnesses, and so is God, how devoutly and justly and blamelessly we behaved toward you who believe,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as you know how we treated each one of you as a father treats his own children,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: appealing to you, encouraging you, and solemnly charging you to walk in a way worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And for this reason we too thank God unceasingly: when you received the word of God that you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of people but as what it truly is, the word of God, which is also at work in you who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you, brothers and sisters, became imitators of the assemblies of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea, because you too suffered the same things from your own compatriots as they did from the Jews

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets and drove us out, who do not please God and are opposed to all people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: preventing us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But the wrath has come upon them at last.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But we, brothers and sisters, orphaned from you for a short time—in person, not in heart—tried all the harder, with great desire, to see you face to face.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, more than once—but Satan blocked us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For what is our hope or joy or crown to boast of before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yes, you are our glory and our joy.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is writing to the whole community. 'Brothers' alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice.

The word can mean 'without result' (the traditional 'in vain') or 'without substance', that is, hollow or insincere. Because the verses that follow defend the missionaries' character and motives and not their success, many scholars prefer the second sense. 'Empty' leaves both open, as the Greek does.

The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' has become a purely religious term and a book title, so the plain meaning is given here. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

The Greek says literally 'to be in weight'. It may mean being a financial burden, as the related verb in verse 9 does, or carrying weight in the sense of insisting on one's authority and importance. Scholars are divided, and Paul may intend both. The rendering keeps 'weight' so that the link with verse 9 remains visible.

Manuscripts are split between 'gentle' (ēpioi) and 'infants' (nēpioi), which differ by a single letter. The edition translated here reads 'gentle', as do most English versions. Many of the earliest manuscripts read 'infants', and some critical editions and scholars prefer that reading as the harder one.

The word usually denotes a wet nurse, a woman employed to suckle and raise another family's children, and a familiar figure of affection in ancient households. The point of 'her own children' is probably that even a professional nurse shows a special tenderness when the children are hers. Some translations simplify to 'nursing mother'.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. The adverb here belongs to that family and describes conduct that is in the right before God and fair toward others.

The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens and, in the Greek Scriptures, the assembled people of Israel. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution, neither of which existed yet. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering, and readers should understand the same communities by 'assembly'.

notes.traditional: the Jews, who killed the Lord Jesus
notes.note: Greek manuscripts have no punctuation here. Most translations place a comma after 'Jews', making what follows a description of the Jewish people as a whole. The Greek construction more naturally identifies a particular group, those who did these things, and the text is rendered that way without a comma. Paul and the Judean assemblies were themselves Jews, and since the setting is Judea some scholars translate 'Judeans'.

The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, Jewish writers used it for all the non-Jewish peoples. English uses 'Gentiles' for that sense and 'nations' elsewhere, but it is one word in Greek.

The phrase can mean 'at last', 'completely' or 'to the end, forever', and translations differ. It is also uncertain what event Paul has in mind, or whether he speaks of a future judgment as so certain that it is already present. A minority of scholars regard verses 13–16 as a later addition, though all manuscripts contain them.

The word means arrival and the presence that follows. In Paul's day it was a standard term for the state visit of a king or emperor to a city, an occasion for celebration and for honours such as crowns. That association fits the crown imagery in this verse.

candidates.reason: The plural address recurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translations vary between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'friends'; it needs one policy.
It is rendered 'soul', 'life' or 'self' across the New Testament, and 'soul' often imports a later body-soul dualism; it needs sense-by-sense guidance.
The Semitic idiom of 'walking' for conduct recurs across Paul and John, and translations split between 'walk' and 'live'.
Translators choose between 'wrath' and 'anger', and the divine-judgment sense recurs in Romans, the Thessalonian letters and Revelation.
The verb and its noun range over 'urge', 'appeal', 'encourage', 'comfort' and 'exhort', and are very frequent; readers cannot otherwise tell it is one word-family.

warnings: Verse 4: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.
